chapters.title: Chapter 4: Valuing Stocks Across the Cycle

lessons.title: Valuing Defensives: Growth, ROCE Durability, and the Cost of Overpaying

body.text: With a defensive, the question is rarely whether the business is good. It is how many years of excellence the share price has already paid for, and whether the high returns on capital that justify that price will survive the next competitor.

children.text: Cyclicals are hard to value because their earnings swing. Defensives are hard to value for the opposite reason: their earnings are so reliable that investors stop asking what they are paying. Chapter 3 showed how a derating can absorb years of growth. This lesson gives you three tools to judge the price before you pay it: how return on capital decides what growth is worth, how to test whether those returns will last, and how to measure the cost of overpaying in years.
Tool 1: Growth Is Only Worth Paying for When Returns Are High

markDefs.definition: Return on Capital Employed: operating profit before interest and tax divided by the total capital used in the business, both equity and debt. It shows how efficiently a company turns capital into profit.

children.text: To grow, a company must reinvest part of its profit. A business with a very high return on equity or

needs to reinvest only a little to grow, so it can pay out most of its profit as well. A business earning just its cost of capital must reinvest almost everything to grow at the same rate, leaving shareholders nothing extra. The formula below captures this, and it explains why investors pay far more for a high-ROCE staples leader than for an ordinary company growing just as fast.

body.caption: g ÷ ROE is the share of profit that must be reinvested to grow at rate g; the rest can be paid out
Same 8% growth, same 11% required return, different ROE (illustrative)

children.text: Read the last two rows together. A company earning exactly its required return is worth 9.8 times earnings growing at 8%, barely more than the 9.1 it would be worth not growing at all. Its growth creates almost no value. The 50% ROE company growing at the same 8% is worth more than three times as much. When you pay a premium for a defensive, you are really paying for the durability of its high returns, not for growth on its own.

body.title: Which Growth Is Worth More?
body.question: Two companies are each expected to grow earnings at 10% a year for many years. Company X earns a 40% ROCE; Company Y earns a 12% ROCE, roughly its cost of capital. Which statement is correct?
options: Both deserve the same P/E, because their growth rates are identical
Company Y deserves a higher P/E, because it reinvests more
Company X deserves a much higher P/E, because it can fund the same growth while paying out far more of its profit
Neither company's P/E depends on ROCE
body.explanation: Company X needs to reinvest only about a quarter of its profit to grow 10%, so most of its earnings are free for shareholders. Company Y must reinvest nearly all its profit to achieve the same growth, and that growth adds little value because it earns only its cost of capital.

children.text: Tool 2: Test Whether High Returns Will Last

If the premium is a payment for durable returns, durability is what you must test. Start with the ROCE history on Screener.in, but read it carefully. A sudden fall does not always mean the business weakened.

stats.label: HUL ROCE, FY22 to FY26
stats.context: After the GSK Consumer Healthcare merger

stats.label: HUL shareholders' equity, FY20 to FY21
HUL cash conversion cycle, FY15 to FY26

children.text: HUL's ROCE collapsed from 117% in FY20 to 39% in FY21 and settled in the high 20s. That was not a business breaking down. The merger with GSK Consumer Healthcare's India business, paid for largely in HUL shares, added tens of thousands of crores of equity, much of it representing brands and goodwill. Capital employed jumped, so the ratio fell, while the underlying soap and detergent business kept its negative working capital and pricing power. The lesson: when ROCE shifts sharply, check the balance sheet for acquisitions before concluding the moat has eroded.

body.caption: What sustains high returns, and what threatens them

cells: Price increases or grammage cuts without market share loss
Well-funded new entrants willing to accept low returns to buy share
Stable or growing market share over many years
New channels such as quick commerce and online platforms that bypass traditional reach
Low capital needs and negative working capital
Negative cash conversion cycle sustained through downturns
Rising trade discounts, longer dealer credit, or heavy new capex
Margins held steady through input cost spikes
Competitors reaching similar scale through large investments

children.text: Case Study: Asian Paints and the Price of Perfection

Asian Paints was, for years, the textbook Indian compounder: dominant market share in decorative paints, ROCE consistently in the 30s and 40s, and a vast dealer network. For FY15 to FY20, the market valued it steadily at roughly 58 to 68 times earnings at the end of each July. Then the post-pandemic enthusiasm pushed the multiple much higher, just before the industry changed.

From Peak Multiple to New Competition

events.title: Share price peaks
events.description: Asian Paints closes at ₹3,576.30, about 109 times its last full-year EPS of ₹32.73 for FY21.

events.title: Birla Opus launches
events.description: The Aditya Birla Group's Grasim Industries launches Birla Opus paints, backed by new plants it described as a 40% addition to industry capacity.

events.title: Earnings fall
events.description: Consolidated EPS falls 32.8%, from ₹56.92 to ₹38.23, amid muted demand and intensifying competition, and ROCE drops from 38% to 26%.

events.title: Partial recovery
events.description: EPS recovers to ₹45.09, but ROCE stays at 26%, well below its historical range.

body.caption: Asian Paints: where the return went, 7 January 2022 peak to 31 July 2026 (price only)

children.text: Two separate things went wrong for anyone who bought at the peak. First, the price: at 109 times earnings, the stock assumed growth would stay exceptional for a very long time. Second, durability: a large, well-funded entrant challenged the returns that justified the premium, and EPS growth slowed to about 6.6% a year from FY21 to FY26, against about 12.5% a year from FY16 to FY21. Even without new competition, the multiple had little room to hold. With it, earnings growth of nearly 38% still left the investor down 23%.
Tool 3: Measure the Cost of Overpaying in Years

A simple way to feel the weight of a high multiple: ask how many years of earnings growth it would take, with the share price going nowhere, for the P/E to fall to a more ordinary level. Those are years in which you earn little beyond dividends while waiting for the business to grow into its price.

body.latex: \text{Years to grow into the price} = \frac{\ln(\text{Current P/E} \div \text{Target P/E})}{\ln(1 + g)}
body.caption: g = annual EPS growth. In Excel or Google Sheets: =LN(current/target)/LN(1+g)
Years of flat share price needed for the P/E to fall to the target

body.title: How Long Is the Wait?
body.prompt: A staples stock trades at 100 times earnings. You think 40 times is a reasonable long-term multiple for it, and you expect EPS to grow 12% a year. If the share price stays flat, how many years would it take for the P/E to fall to 40? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ln(100 ÷ 40) ÷ ln(1.12) = 0.916 ÷ 0.113 = about 8.1 years. For eight years, even strong 12% earnings growth would only be catching the business up to its price. If growth slows to 8%, the wait stretches to about 11.9 years.

columns.label: A premium is reasonable when
points: ROCE is high and has been stable through past slowdowns and cost spikes
Market share is steady or rising, with no large well-funded entrant
The P/E is near or below the stock's own long-term median
It would take only a few years of expected growth to grow into the price

columns.label: You are likely overpaying when
points: The P/E is far above its own history after a period of enthusiasm
ROCE is falling for business reasons, not acquisition accounting
New competitors are adding significant capacity or discounting heavily
It would take a decade or more of strong growth just to reach a normal multiple

body.title: Quality at Any Price?
body.scenario: Arjun, a mutual fund investor who also buys a few stocks directly, wants to add a premium consumer company to his portfolio for stability. It trades at 80 times earnings, against a 10-year median of about 55. Its ROCE has slipped from 45% to 32% over three years, with no major acquisition. Two large conglomerates have entered its category in the last 18 months. Management expects 12% annual EPS growth. Arjun says: 'It's the best company in its sector, so the valuation doesn't matter over the long term.'
body.prompt: Apply the three tools from this lesson. What would you tell Arjun?
body.modelAnswer: Tool 1: its ROCE is still well above the cost of capital, so growth does create value, but a fall from 45% to 32% means each rupee of growth is worth less than before. Tool 2: the ROCE decline has no acquisition to explain it and coincides with two well-funded entrants, which is a warning that the source of high returns may be under pressure, similar to what happened in decorative paints. Tool 3: even if management delivers 12% growth, it would take about ln(80 ÷ 55) ÷ ln(1.12), roughly 3.3 years of flat price just to return to the median multiple, and about 6.1 years to reach 40. If competition slows growth to 8%, those waits stretch to about 4.9 and 9.0 years. Valuation matters a great deal for a long-term investor when the starting multiple is high and durability is in question. Arjun could wait for a lower price, size the position small, or look for a defensive whose ROCE is stable and whose valuation is closer to its history.

body.title: Valuing a Defensive Before You Buy
steps: Pull 10 years of ROCE from Screener.in's Ratios section and note the range and trend
If ROCE shifted sharply, check the balance sheet for acquisitions or large equity issues before drawing conclusions
Check the cash conversion cycle for signs of rising dealer credit or inventory
Scan recent earnings calls and industry news for new entrants, capacity additions, and discounting
Compare the current P/E with the stock's own 10-year median
Calculate the years of expected EPS growth needed for the P/E to reach its median, and again with growth 3 to 4 points lower
Decide whether you are paying for durable returns or for a best-case scenario

points: Growth is only valuable when returns on capital are well above the cost of capital; a company earning just its required return gains little value from growing
A defensive's premium is really a payment for the durability of its high ROCE
Sharp ROCE changes can come from acquisition accounting, as with HUL after the GSK Consumer Healthcare merger, so check the balance sheet before concluding the moat has weakened
Asian Paints showed both risks together: a peak P/E of about 109 and a well-funded new entrant, so EPS rose 37.8% while the share price fell 23.2%
Translate a high P/E into years: how long strong growth must run with a flat price just to reach a normal multiple
Paying up is reasonable when returns are stable and the multiple is near its history; it becomes overpaying when both conditions fail

body.text: HUL and Asian Paints figures are consolidated annual data as displayed on Screener.in at the time of writing and may be restated. Share prices are daily closes from historical market data; returns exclude dividends. The justified P/E and years-to-normalise calculations are simplified models, and the ROE examples and Arjun's scenario are illustrative. References to listed companies are for education only and are not recommendations to buy or sell any security.
